summary: A conversational podcast-style interview capturing Spark Labs' journey with Redwood Inference. Focused on production wins (latency, cost), migration story from a homegrown stack, and promotional permissions for quotes and a case study. Friendly, informal tone; marketing and engineering both present.
topics: customer success story and marketing permission
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining—happy Tuesday. Uh so quick roll call?
[00:07] Amir (Spark Labs): Amir here, hey Maya, hey all.
[00:09] Janelle (Spark Labs): Janelle on from Boston, hi.
[00:11] Roberto (Spark Labs): Roberto, morning.
[00:13] Noah (Redwood): Noah here.
[00:14] Sofia (Redwood Marketing): Sofia, hi!
[00:16] Maya: Great. We're recording this for a short podcast case piece; if anyone wants to opt out say so now.
[00:22] Amir: No opt-out, go for it.
[00:24] Maya: Awesome. So this is pretty informal — we'll talk through your story with Redwood, how you decided to move from the in-house inference stack, the big wins, and then we'll grab a few quotable moments for a landing page. Sound good?
[00:35] Janelle: Sounds good.
[00:36] Roberto: Yep.
[00:37] [00:37] Maya: Great. Maybe, Amir, can you kick off with a 90-second origin story — how Spark Labs got started and where ML fits in?
[00:45] Amir: Sure. Uh Spark Labs started in 2018, we build developer tooling for realtime analytics and...uh, eventually moved into generative features for code and docs. By 2024 we had a small inference stack in-house — mostly CPUs, a little GPU — it was fine for prototyping, but, you know, as usage grew we started hitting tail latency and cost problems. We had an SSE-ish team building batching layer but it was, it was fragile.
[01:12] Maya: When you say tail latency, can you unpack that a bit—what were you seeing?
[01:18] Amir: Yeah, so p99s like 1.5 to 2 seconds for typical doc generation requests at peak, and sometimes we saw 3-4s when KV caching would, like, misalign. People blamed network or the KV cache but it ended up being the way we scheduled requests. Also cost per 1k requests climbed because we couldn't leverage batching well across customers.
[01:38] [00:00:00.00] Noah (Redwood SE): (slight overlap) And you were on a patched together queue, right? Not a dedicated serving runtime?
[00:43] Amir: Exactly. It was Rabbit MQ plus a few homegrown helpers.
[00:46] Maya: Janelle, what was the business trigger for exploring Redwood?
[00:50] Janelle: Two things: we wanted consistent latencies for our interactive features, and we wanted to not have to babysit infra during launches. We also had a compliance ask for audit logs for the enterprise tier which our in-house tooling didn't capture well.
[01:05] Maya: Nice, nice. Roberto, walk us through the migration checklist—what were the big technical concerns?
[01:11] Roberto: Oh, a lot. Model compatibility was the first—some of our models had custom attention layers, we were worried about losing fidelity with quantized variants. Also routing — we needed sticky sessions for some customers to ensure personalization state wasn't lost, and encryption / KMS integration because we handle PII-ish metadata.
[01:29] Noah: Quick clarifier — you used Redwood Hosted first, is that right?
[01:32] Amir: Yeah, we onboarded to hosted API first to validate behavior. We did a two-week pilot with a 2k request/day baseline, then spiked to 30k/day during a feature beta.
[01:41] Maya: Can you share the first quantifiable win you remember?
[01:44] Amir: Sure — after switching to Redwood we saw median latency drop from about 350ms to ~120ms for our most common prompt shape, p95 improved from 1.2s to 230-250ms. Cost per 1k requests dropped, uh, I want to say ~28% after batching and the prefix cache kicked in.
[02:07] Janelle: Adding to that — the auto-batching that Redwood suggested meant we stopped over-provisioning GPU nodes for burst. That alone saved us operational headaches.
[02:17] Maya: Were there any surprises — like something that didn't go as expected?
[02:20] Amir: The first week we saw a slight regression in one model variant — I think it was because our model used a different tokenizer edge-case; we had to pin a model version and Redwood's SE worked with us to add a compatibility shim.
[02:32] Roberto: Also a small hiccup integrating our KMS — we use a HSM-backed key manager and the handshake needed an extra IP allowlist step. But support was responsive.
[02:42] [00:02:42] Sofia: (chiming in) For marketing, Amir, can I ask — what's a short phrase you'd use to describe the impact Redwood had for Spark Labs?
[02:49] Amir: Hmm. Maybe "Made inference predictable and cheap enough to productize." But that's clunky.
[02:54] Janelle: I like "predictable and production-ready inference".
[02:57] Amir: Yeah, okay I can sign off on that.
[02:59] Maya: Great — we'll use that as a starter for the blurb. We'll send an approval doc.
[03:04] [00:03:04] Noah: Can I ask a technical question — you mentioned batching—how did your prompt shapes change, any pattern we should call out?
[03:11] Roberto: Mostly shorter prompts with repeated header context. We restructured prompts to surface more instruction up front so the batching window could aggregate similar-length requests.
[03:22] Noah: Did you use Redwood's KV cache for personalization?
[03:25] Amir: Yes, but we had to adjust cache TTLs. Early on we had K-V cash TTLs too long and then personalization lagged. Learned to keep short TTL for session keys and longer for rarely changing user prefs.
[03:39] Maya: Nice. Audience question — competition: did you consider Anthropic or AWS endpoints?
[03:45] Amir: We evaluated Anthropic for safety features and OpenAI for access, but cost and control pushed us to Redwood. AWS was attractive but we wanted a vendor that focused on inference ergonomics rather than infra plumbing.
[03:59] Janelle: And Redwood's rollout features — canary and automatic fallbacks — were good for our beta.
[04:06] [00:04:06] Sofia: On the case study side, any metrics you're comfortable sharing publicly? We already heard p95 & cost uplift, anything else — user engagement changes?
[04:14] Amir: Engagement on the new feature increased DAU retention by about 6% in the week following launch. Also error rate dropped; we had fewer timeouts so customer-facing errors were down ~40%.
[04:26] Maya: That's great. We'll surface those with attribution notes.
[04:29] [00:04:29] Janelle: One more technical note — we used Redwood Optimize suggestions to pick a quantized model for lower-cost inference. The evals were helpful; the only time accuracy dropped was in one niche prompt, and we decided to route those to a higher-fidelity variant.
[04:45] Noah: That routing policy — was it automatic or manual?
[04:48] Janelle: Initially manual, then we added a simple rule based on prompt tag that triggered fallback to the high-fidelity model.
[04:55] Noah: Cool.
[04:56] [00:04:56] Maya: Okay some softer questions: was there anything about working with Redwood that surprised your team culturally or process-wise?
[05:02] Amir: I was pleasantly surprised by the cross-functional pairing — our PM and Redwood's solutions engineer actually did a joint runbook session which helped us adopt run-time observability faster.
[05:13] Roberto: And the docs had decent examples, not perfect but good starting points.
[05:18] [00:05:18] Sofia: (laughing) We'll take the docs as a compliment.
[05:21] Maya: For the podcast — any stories or anecdotes you want to put on the record?
[05:25] Amir: There's one quick story — during our big beta we were doing a midnight deployment and we saw a sudden p99 spike. Our on-call noticed, flipped the routing policy to a cheaper variant and the site stayed up; we joked that Redwood saved our engineers from a midnight pizza run. That might be a fun line.
[05:41] Sofia: Love it. We'll probably use that in social.
[05:44] Janelle: (softly) Midnight pizza saved by Redwood.
[05:47] [00:05:47] Maya: (laugh) Great. Switching gears — for quote approvals, Sofia will send a short doc. Amir if you could confirm — are you okay with the quote "predictable and production-ready inference" and the engagement metrics mentioned?
[05:59] Amir: Yes, I'm good with that, and with the numbers as long as we attribute the timeframe and cohorts.
[06:05] Sofia: We'll include exact cohorts and timeframe in the approval doc.
[06:08] [00:06:08] Maya: Any legal or procurement red flags for marketing content?
[06:12] Janelle: Just standard compliance checks — we can't share any PII and we'll need to anonymize internal customer names.
[06:19] Maya: Understood. We'll scrub before publishing.
[06:22] Amir: Also, please don't mention the customer's company name in the anecdote without permission.
[06:26] Maya: We won't.
[06:28] [00:06:28] Noah: Technical aside — do you still run any inference on-prem for compliance?
[06:33] Amir: We keep a small on-prem deployment for a handful of enterprise customers, but the main traffic is through Redwood Hosted with private VPC peering for data flows.
[06:43] Roberto: We liked that Redwood offered a Private option if needed; that gave procurement confidence.
[06:48] [00:06:48] Maya: Nice. Audience again: any product features you'd like Redwood to build?
[06:53] Janelle: Better guidance on tokenizer edge cases — we hit one where a custom tokenization produced shifted logits. A checklist for tokenization compatibility would be great.
[07:02] Amir: Also deeper guardrails around safety for user-generated content. We rely on Anthropic's safety research but would love integrated evals.
[07:12] Noah: Good feedback — we'll pass that on.
[07:15] [00:07:15] Sofia: Quick marketing note — do you have a preference for distribution channels? We do a written case study + 20-min audio snippet + 60-second social.
[07:24] Amir: Audio + short write-up is perfect. Maybe include a technical appendix for developer readers.
[07:31] Maya: We can do a small appendix with anonymized throughput/latency numbers and a note about quantization choices.
[07:39] [00:07:39] Roberto: That would help our engineers evaluate tradeoffs.
[07:42] Maya: Great. Any final tech tips for teams considering migrating?
[07:46] Amir: Start with a small pilot on your most common prompt shape, measure p95 and cost, and don't try to move everything at once. Also, have a migration playbook with rollback hooks.
[07:58] Janelle: And test tokenization early.
[08:00] [00:08:00] Noah: Awesome. We usually recommend a canary rollout and traffic mirroring when possible.
[08:07] Maya: We're nearing the 30-minute mark so we'll wrap with a quick recap and confirm next steps.
[08:12] Sofia: Before we wrap — Amir, anything you'd like to promote from Spark Labs? A code snippet or demo for readers?
[08:18] Amir: We have a short demo repo showing how we do prompt shaping for batching, open-source on GitHub, we'll link that in the case study.
[08:27] Maya: Perfect. Alright recap: Sofia sends approval doc and promotional timeline; Maya uploads recording; Noah shares a short performance spreadsheet; Amir approves the quote and provides demo repo link. Any changes?
[08:41] Janelle: All good.
[08:42] Roberto: Good.
[08:43] Amir: Good.
[08:44] Maya: Thanks everyone—we'll follow up with dates. We'll stop recording now but feel free to keep chatting.
[08:50] [00:08:50] (recording stops)

Notes about transcript quality: automated captions had a few mis-hearings of technical terms ("KV cache" as "K-V cash", "quantized" sometimes as "quanta-sized") and some overlapping talk around 00:02:42 and 00:05:18.
